newsitem.title: GERMANY: German opposition SPD looks to Britain's Blair.
newsitem.headline: German opposition SPD looks to Britain's Blair.

text.p: If the Labour Party wins Thursday's British general election, members of Germany's Social Democrats could be forgiven a wistful sigh in the direction of their television screens as they watch Tony Blair celebrate.
Like Blair's new Labour, the SPD faces the challenge of ousting a party which has been in power so long that a whole generation cannot remember any other government.
Sadly for the SPD, many commentators say, the similarities end there.

The party does not have a charismatic leader like Blair and it faces a far more formidable opponent in Chancellor Helmut Kohl's Christian Democrats than Labour has in Prime Minister John Major's squabbling Conservatives.
SPD members, however, are hoping a Labour victory and a successful first year in government can give them a boost as they bid to unseat Kohl, in power since 1982, next autumn.

"If their programme takes off and people on the continent see things are changing for the better -- perhaps with a shift in European policy -- that could have a more positive effect for the SPD," said researcher Frank Karl of the Friedrich Ebert Institute, a Bonn-based think tank with close links to the SPD.
But while Labour and the SPD stem from the same political family, Blair would appear to have no obvious German cousins.
"Tony Blair is incomparable. He's a one-off," said Karl, who had the opportunity to observe the Labour leader at first hand during a recent visit to London.
Neither SPD leader Oskar Lafontaine nor Gerhard Schroeder, his main rival to run for the chancellery, can pull off the sort of dramatic facelift Blair has carried out with Labour.

"A big turnaround like that is not possible in the SPD because it's already happened with the Godesberg programme," said Professor Thomas Meyer of Dortmund University, referring to the SPD's own modernisation drive -- which dates back to 1959.
Some German media have speculated that a victory for the ever-smiling Blair could boost the fortunes of Schroeder, the media-friendly and pro-business premier of Lower Saxony state.
"He laughs just as often as Blair and has the almost the same views on economic policy," Bild am Sonntag noted.
"But in contrast to Blair, Schroeder is an outsider in his own party," the weekly added, noting the maverick politician could only run for chancellor with Lafontaine's agreement.
Meyer said the question of who within the SPD could benefit most from a Blair victory remained open and depended on what kind of policies the Labour leader pursued in office.
"It depends if Blair is successful and uses his media presence just to pursue conservative policies or if he uses his power to actually push through a Social Democratic programme."
Success for more identifiably left-wing policies could favour Lafontaine, who is viewed as closer to the left and a master of balancing the various factions within the SPD.
But perhaps the most important factor to bear in mind in assessing the SPD's chances in the light of a Labour victory is its opponent -- Germany's longest-serving postwar chancellor.
"Compared to John Major, Kohl stands at the head of a united party," the Sueddeutsche Zeitung daily wrote in an editorial.

"Apart from the fact that the German Social Democrats do not have a Blair-like figure, they should remember how little their opponent, the German head of government, has in common with his colleague in Downing Street," the liberal paper said.
